title: Truth, Verification & Critical Thinking — Module Quiz

items.q: Why does fluent text suppress scepticism?
options: Fluent text is usually more accurate
Fluency has always signalled effort, and generated text breaks that link while keeping the signal
People do not read carefully enough
items.explain: Your reading instincts were built when effortful writing indicated an effortful writer. That correlation is now severed and will not update on its own.

items.q: Specificity — names, dates, percentages — indicates:
options: That someone checked the claim
Nothing about accuracy; detail is as cheap to generate as vagueness
A more capable model was used
items.explain: Fabricated citations are specific by construction. Specificity feels like verification and is not.

items.q: The right response to unreliable fluency is:
options: Doubt everything an assistant produces
Spend scepticism where being wrong costs something
Use assistants only for creative work
items.explain: Uniform doubt is exhausting and gets abandoned within days. A budget spent on consequential claims survives a working week.

items.q: The two triage questions are:
options: Is it interesting, and is it well written?
What happens if it is wrong, and how easily could it be undone?
Is it recent, and is it detailed?
items.explain: Consequence and reversibility together identify the minority of claims worth a limited budget.

items.q: Which category should always be checked before use?
options: General explanations of how something works
Citations and references
Suggestions for further reading
items.explain: A plausible author, journal and year with no such paper is the classic failure. Never repeat a citation you have not opened.

items.q: Why check an answer that is unusually convenient?
options: Convenient answers are usually fabricated
It is the answer you will not scrutinise, so an error there travels furthest
Models are designed to flatter users
items.explain: The risk is in your own reaction rather than the model's intent — you stop looking when the answer suits you.

items.q: Why is asking 'are you sure?' not verification?
options: Models cannot assess outputs at all
The same process produces both answer and reassurance, and models concede under pressure
It consumes another message
items.explain: Agreement is not confirmation, and pushing back on a correct answer often produces an apology and a wrong one.

items.q: Lateral reading means:
options: Reading further down the same page
Leaving the page to see what other sources say about it
Comparing several claims side by side
items.explain: A professional-looking site is easy to produce, so reading more of it proves nothing. This is what fact-checkers actually do.

items.q: The most common verification failure is discovering that:
options: The source was entirely fabricated
The source is real but the claim was detached from its conditions
The source is paywalled
items.explain: The study exists and covered a different population; the clause applies above a threshold. More common than invention and harder to notice.

items.q: Which property most reliably indicates a source cares about accuracy?
options: Professional design and a recognised name
It publishes corrections
It is never seen to be wrong
items.explain: Everyone is sometimes wrong. A source that never appears to be is one that does not tell you.

items.q: "Who benefits if I believe this?" is asked to:
options: Identify conspiracies
Make incentives visible, so a claim matching them gets a second source
Decide which sources can be dismissed
items.explain: Everyone has incentives, including good sources. The question is whether they are visible and whether the claim is what they would predict.

items.q: Institutional authority should be used to:
options: Decide what is true
Decide where to look first
Rank sources definitively
items.explain: Authority is a weak signal. Signals point you somewhere; evidence decides what you conclude.

items.q: The most common reason two credible sources disagree:
options: One of them is wrong
They measured different things
One is deliberately misleading
items.explain: "Unemployment" and "users" have several definitions. Two correct numbers can describe two different quantities.

items.q: False balance is:
options: Declining to take a position
Presenting a lopsided disagreement as an even contest
Citing only one side of a debate
items.explain: Assistants default to it because they are trained to appear balanced. Ask about the distribution of support, not just the positions.

items.q: When a question is genuinely unsettled, the honest response is:
options: Pick the better-supported side and state it plainly
Say it is unresolved and say what would settle it
Avoid the question entirely
items.explain: Manufacturing certainty to sound decisive is the failure. Naming what would resolve it is more useful than an invented conclusion.

items.q: Why is 'watch for bad grammar' obsolete scam advice?
options: Attackers now hire proofreaders
Fluent text in any language is free to produce
Mail clients correct spelling automatically
items.explain: The tell existed because attackers often did not write your language natively. That is no longer a constraint.

items.q: An out-of-band check means:
options: Asking the sender to confirm who they are
Contacting the real person through a channel and number you already had
Checking the sender's domain spelling
items.explain: It does not require judging the message, so it defeats even a perfect voice clone — the attacker does not control your address book.

items.q: Which pairing is the strongest warning sign?
options: A long message with attachments
Urgency combined with secrecy
An unfamiliar sender address
items.explain: Urgency prevents you thinking and secrecy keeps you from the person who would notice. Both are structural, so better fakery does not remove them.

items.q: Asymmetric scrutiny is:
options: Checking some sources more carefully than others
Checking claims you dislike thoroughly and claims you like barely at all
Applying different standards to different subjects
items.explain: Both feel like normal reading, yet two claims of identical reliability received completely different standards.

items.q: Why does knowing about confirmation bias not reduce it?
options: It is not a genuine effect
It operates before you notice, so only changed procedure helps
It affects only untrained readers
items.explain: The feeling of being fair-minded is unrelated to whether you are. What helps is something that does not depend on catching yourself.

items.q: Deciding in advance what would change your mind works because:
options: It commits you publicly
You set the standard before knowing which way the evidence went
It makes research faster
items.explain: Afterwards the standard moves — you find reasons the evidence you found is not quite the evidence you meant.

items.q: Which statement is strongest?
options: "It's about 15%, but don't quote me"
"15% for the UK in 2025 from the ONS release, which I checked; I have not confirmed the other markets"
items.explain: Naming what you checked and what you did not tells the reader how much weight to place on it. Vagueness is not humility.

items.q: E7 is compulsory for certification because:
options: It is the longest module
Every other module assumes it — without it the curriculum makes you an efficient source of confident errors
Verification is a legal requirement
items.explain: Faster is only good if the output is right. E4's routine, E5's documents and E6's disclosure all assume you can check.

items.q: A primary source is:
options: The most authoritative article about a subject
The thing itself — the paper, the legislation, the filing, the dataset
The first search result
items.explain: Every layer between you and the source is a layer where a qualifier was dropped.
